newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian official agrees logging problems linger.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian official agrees logging problems linger.

text.p: Logging continues unabated in Cambodia despite a government directive banning all log exports from December 31, government officials said on Monday.
"Unfortunately, yes," said Minister of Finance Keat Chhon when asked whether charges from a British environmental group earlier on Monday were true.
Global Witness, in a briefing paper titled "A Tug of War, the struggle to preserve Cambodia's forests", has criticised the government's management of "quasi-legal" logging concessions.
It alleged continued government involvement in illegal logging and questioned the administration's commitment to reforming forestry policy.
"We have to work hard so that this government can organise its natural resources in a proper way," Keat Chhon told reporters after opening a seminar on the ASEAN Free Trade Area.

The criticisms came soon after Minister of Environment Mok Mareth expressed concern over logging activities in Cambodian national parks. They also coincide with an International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission now reviewing Cambodia's forestry policy.
The IMF delegation is due to determine the fate of $40 million in loans due to Cambodia after the fund cancelled a $20 million payment last year over the logging issue.

Keat Chhon said he remained hopeful about the IMF loan despite continued logging practices because the government was committed to greater fiscal discipline, natural resources management and civil service reform.
Co-Premier Hun Sen warned last Tuesday that Cambodia would have to resume cutting and selling logs if the IMF cut the loan because it needed the money to pay civil servants.
Keat Chhon, however, said of Hun Sen's comments: "No such scenario will happen."
Global Witness described Hun Sen's comments as an ultimatum that called into question whether the government's commitment to forestry reform was slipping.
